text: In 1972, Wall Street found stocks it said you would never have to sell.
Two years later, one of them had lost about ninety percent of its value. It wasn't a penny stock. It was Polaroid.
This is Walt. He isn't a real person. He's built from the choices real professional investors made in 1972.
Walt is about to put his clients' retirement money into the most admired companies in America, and promise never to sell.
By the end of this story, you'll know whether he was right, and the one number that decided it.
November fourteenth, 1972. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closes above one thousand for the first time in its history.
Walt runs a pension fund. The money belongs to people like Ruth, who spent thirty-one years on a factory line, and now counts on that pension every month.
Two years earlier, a bear market had wrecked the speculative go-go stocks of the 1960s. Professionals like Walt wanted the opposite. Big, famous, dependable companies.
And professionals were now the biggest buyers in the market. Bank trust departments, pension funds and mutual funds poured money into the same few dozen names.

There was never an official list. But the names kept repeating. IBM. Coca-Cola. McDonald's. Disney. Xerox. Avon. Philip Morris. And Polaroid, which had just launched the SX-70, a camera that ejected a photo that developed before your eyes.
Wall Street called them one-decision stocks. You made one decision, to buy. And then you never had to think about it again.
For a professional, it was the perfect investment, one you could always defend. And for a while, it worked.
But there is one number that tells you how much hope is already built into a stock's price. The price-to-earnings ratio, or P E.
If a company earns one dollar per share in a year, and the stock costs fifteen dollars, the P E is fifteen. You're paying fifteen dollars for each dollar of yearly profit.
At the end of 1972, the S and P 500 traded at about nineteen times earnings.
McDonald's traded at about eighty-six. Polaroid, at more than ninety.
On average, the Nifty Fifty cost about forty-two times earnings. Roughly double the rest of the market.

At more than ninety times earnings, Polaroid would need more than ninety years of its 1972 profits to earn back the price of one share. That price only made sense if the company grew fast, for decades, without stumbling.
Walt saw the numbers. He decided quality was worth any price.
By 1973, the press had a name for it. A two-tier market. A small club of favorites at the top, and everything else below. Then almost everything went wrong.

The first domino had tipped back in August 1971, when President Nixon stopped exchanging dollars for gold with foreign governments. By early 1973, the system of fixed exchange rates built after World War Two had broken down.
Prices were already rising. Loose money, a global jump in food prices, and the end of wage and price controls all pushed inflation higher.

Then, in October 1973, Arab oil producers announced an embargo against the United States. By January, the price of oil had nearly quadrupled, from about three dollars a barrel to almost twelve. Americans waited in long lines for gas.
By the end of 1974, consumer prices were rising more than twelve percent a year. To fight it, the Federal Reserve pushed interest rates sharply higher.

Here is why that mattered for the Nifty Fifty. When interest rates rise, profits promised far in the future are worth less today. Stocks priced on decades of growth have the most to lose. The higher the P E, the further the fall.
The economy slipped into recession in late 1973. And in August 1974, Watergate forced Nixon to resign.
On Walt's desk, a letter from Ruth. Just one question. Is my pension safe?
The S and P 500 had peaked on January eleventh, 1973. By October third, 1974, it had fallen forty-eight percent. The worst bear market since the 1930s.
The favorites fell even harder. Each from its own peak, Xerox fell about seventy-one percent. Avon, about eighty-six. And Polaroid, about ninety-one.
Many of these companies were still selling their products. What collapsed was the price investors were willing to pay.

October 1974. The bottom. Walt's boss wants out, before it gets any worse. Walt holds the key to the lock he promised never to open. Sell, and the loss is locked in. Hold, and it might get worse. What would you do?

Here is what waiting meant. The S and P 500's price didn't get back to its 1973 peak until July 1980. Counting dividends, investors were back to even by about 1976. But after inflation, it took until around 1985. Roughly twelve years.
So, were the Nifty Fifty a terrible investment? Economists still argue about it.

In 1998, Wharton professor Jeremy Siegel asked what would have happened if you had bought them at the very top, and held. His answer. About twelve point two percent a year, through August 1998. The S and P 500 returned about twelve point seven. Close, but still behind.
A few winners carried the group. Philip Morris, one of the cheaper names at about twenty-four times earnings, became one of the best stocks of the era.

But in 2002, economists Jeff Fesenmaier and Gary Smith pointed out that there was never one official list. They took the stocks that appeared on two different lists from 1972, and found that those core favorites ended 2001 with roughly half the wealth of the S and P 500.
And Polaroid, one of the most expensive of all, filed for bankruptcy in 2001.
The two studies disagree on a lot. But they agree on what matters most. The more investors paid for each dollar of earnings in 1972, the worse they tended to do afterward.
Today, the ten largest companies make up about thirty-eight percent of the S and P 500.
Estimates for the early 1970s range from about twenty-two to thirty percent. By that measure, the market is more top-heavy now than at the height of the Nifty Fifty.
Today's giants are dominant and enormously profitable. So were many of the Nifty Fifty.
None of this means a crash is coming. Nobody can predict when markets turn. But it is worth asking the question Walt never asked.
1985. Walt finally writes back to Ruth. He knows now what went wrong in 1972.
They called them one-decision stocks. And in a way, there really was only one decision that mattered. Not whether to buy. Not whether to sell. But how much you were willing to pay.
So before you buy anything that everyone calls a sure thing, look at what you are paying for each dollar it earns.
